title: GitHub actions
body:
This PR introduces GitHub Actions into the repo. The actions perform the following steps:

* Creates a conda environment using the environment.yml and requirements.txt and requirements-develop.txt
  * The environment packages are cached to allow for faster remote runs
* Builds the documentation with `sphinx`
  * Note that the documentation is not currently deployed
* Checks code quality with `flake8` and `black`
* Runs the `pytest` tests

Two workflows are created - they run the same steps but one runs on a self-hosted runner (for pull requests to master and develop) and the other runs on the shared runner (for pushes to master and develop). I will write a gist for setting up the self-hosted runner before marking this PR as ready.

Closes #8

title: Add structural module with simple beam finite element model

closes #29 

This is an initial pass, in which I have gotten rid of `Loop` and `Shell` from the old `BLUEPRINT` `beams` module and attempted to use primitive geometry (`BluemiraFace`) and `Coordinates` instead.

I have gotten rid of the link to `sectionproperties` for now, meaning that this implementation does not have access to cross-sectional properties calculated by finite element, and only has analytical properties. This is because `sectionproperties` has recently had a major version update, and I wanted to get in at least a basic working version of this before revisiting FE XS properties at a later date.

NOTE: I have left sectionproperties as a dependency because it is used elswhere.

The major downside is that torsional properties (in particular, `J`) does not have a closed form analytical solution.

title: Implement Component in bluemira
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
BLUEPRINT uses arbitrary dictionaries to represent components of reactor systems, which leads to a proliferation of objects that quickly become difficult to navigate.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The mirapy `Component` class introduces a tree structure to navigate through the different components that make up a reactor system (and ultimately a reactor). It could be that we can also remove `ReactorSystem` and just build a tree of `Component` objects to represent a given reactor. The `Component` classes will likely need to be parameterised using the `Parameter` and `ParameterFrame` classes. We may need to temporarily allow the shape of a `Component` to be represented by a `Loop` or `Shell` in order to migrate BLUEPRINT functionality.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
If we were to migrate the BLUEPRINT `ReactorSystem` classes as-is, then we would lose the benefits introduced by the tree structure and would need to come up with a separate class-based representation of the `geom` dictionaries anyway. It is likely such an implementation would ultimately end up looking like a `Component` in any case.

FYI @ivanmaione @CoronelBuendia

title: Implement Parameter and ParameterFrame in bluemira
body:
This is a placeholder issue, pending discussion of the base class architecture for bluemira, to be had on 18th June.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
We need a way to efficiently track parameters as they flow through the reactor design, and to store their associated metadata. We also need to be able to interface that data with the outside world e.g. by passing json into / out of bluemira, and passing data from bluemira to external dependencies.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
BLUEPRINT's `ParameterFrame` and enclosed `Parameter` classes provide a means to both define the parameters that are required to parameterise a component in the reactor design and to pass that information around between the different components. They can also be exported / imported as json to naturally build out our interfaces. There are pending changes in BLUEPRINT that should be included as part of this migration.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We may eventually want to up-lift `Parameter`s and `ParameterFrame`s as dataclasses (or e.g. a pydantics equivalent). In order to expedite this migration, it is likely best to move things in their current state (with pending BLUEPRINT changes applied) and then perform any further uplifts in-place.

FYI @ivanmaione @CoronelBuendia

title: Remove BLUEPRINT typechecking
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
We currently have a homebrew type checking framework in BLUEPRINT. This adds a maintenance overhead for functionality that is less relevant to BLUEPRINT's purpose and it is planned to not port this over to bluemira, so we should remove this functionality so that it doesn't need to be maintained while we merge other functionality.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Remove BLUEPRINT/base/typebase.py and resolve associated impact from other files e.g. baseclass.py to ensure functionality works without the type checking.

This approach would be isolated to impact on the BLUEPRINT codebase only.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
There is a longer term plan to implement [`pydantic`](https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io/) to handle type parsing, but implementing that has a longer lead time than would be acceptable for the initial bluemira merge.

FYI @CoronelBuendia

The mirapy `meshing` module interfaces mirapy `Shape1D` (wires) with the python GMSH API to generate meshes that can be read by meshio and imported into common FEM solvers as Fenics and FreeFEM. It can be adapted for bluemira creating the interface for `BluemiraWire` objects. However we should rethink the use of `lcar` property (as in mirapy `Shape`) since it could create confusion due to the "container" nature of `BluemiraWire` objects.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
- FreeCAD implements some meshing methods that use GMSH or NETGEN to mesh FreeCAD topological data. However such methods are well integrated into the GUI but difficult to use in a python script (they are strongly interfaced with some GUI options as the selection one). That would require a strong effort.

**Additional context**
It would be worth considering the use of `pygmsh` library instead of the native GMSH python API. Under evaluation.

FYI @DanShort12 @CoronelBuendia

title: Add ComponentManager
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
We introduce Component trees into bluemira under #58. However, a reactor build will generate multiple trees, for example when working across multiple coordinate systems. In this case, we need some way to get the overall picture for a given component across the different trees (e.g. a `find_component` function).

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I propose to implement a new class `ComponentManager` that will be a property of the various analyses / builders used to encode the design methods for a reactor study. The analyses and builders would make use of the `ComponentManager` to assign components to each tree tag (e.g. csys).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A potentially simpler solution could be to use an unmanaged dictionary to fulfil this functionality, but it is likely that we will want to encapsulate some behaviour of the component management to avoid different scenarios needing to how to find a particular component.

title: Proposal: Validate dependency changes in ComponentManager
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
When we perform a reactor design analysis, we will make various updates to different components and how those components are reflected in the different component trees. This introduces the potential scenario where a component is built, a dependent component is also built, the original component is updated. In this case the second component will be inconsistent with the first. As long as the updates are made via the relevant `ComponentManager`, it should be possible to detect that a dependency has changed and to alert the user that a component is 'dirty' when it is next accessed.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The `ComponentManager` should have utilities for accessing and updating components in their relevant trees and also for identifying dependencies between components (for example as supplied via the relevant builder class). Dependant components should be marked as dirty when a dependency is updated, and should be marked as clean again when the dependant component is rebuilt.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
It would be difficult to manage such dependencies outside of a manager class.

title: Proposal: Introduce an abstract builder class
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Different reactor design studies will encapsulate different build logic, which will need to be reflected in classes that know how to build the relevant components. These classes will need to be aware of the parameters and build settings being used to define the analysis, the components that they produce with any dependencies, and the coordinate systems and other tags that would be used to associate components with their relevant tree. It should also be possible to select the builder class to use in a particular analysis via the user's configuration.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We should introduce a builder class that reflects the functionality of the BLUEPRINT `ReactorSystem`. Initially, we should contain the different methods and properties of that builder functionality in an abstract class, which can then be used as a basis on which to define the builder classes for different components and systems.

title: Proposal: Introduce an abstract Analysis class
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
A given reactor design study will perform various tasks to build components, analyse the behaviour of those systems, and to coordinate the state of the various component trees. A particular study can be encoded by an `Analysis` class, for which an abstract class should exist as a template for any study.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We should implement an abstract `Analysis` class to act as a basis for design studies - the functionality would be similar to the `Reactor` class in BLUEPRINT. The `Analysis` class should be aware of the relevant configuration being used (parameters, build configuration, build tweaks) and will act as the highest level API into bluemira for executing a design study. It should be possible for a user to be able to select the specific `Analysis` that they will use via their configuration.

title: Implement a serialize/deserialize function for geometry objects
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
In the present implementation of bluemira it is not possible to extract curve parameters (e.g. start and end points of a line, or poles of a bezier curve) without accessing directly the freecad object. I would like to have a method that interfaces with freecad and serialize/deserialize bluemira geometry objects.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Implement in `_freecadapi.py` and `tools.py` a set of methods that extract wire's curve parameters from the freecad object. These methods should return a dictionary with all the information necessary to restore the initial object.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Instead of using a dictionary, it would also have been possible to create a set of bluemira primitive classes (e.g. Line, Circle, BSpline, Bezier, etc.) in which essential primitive information is stored. Serialize and Deserialize methods would have been then added to such classes. However, the time requested for such implementation could take more time.

**Additional context**
-

title: Proposal: Refactor of default params logic
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Currently BLUEPRINT-style parameters are based off of a set of templates for each class, which are defined via a record list using a set of default values and metadata. The metadata, serialisation, and ability to copy through parameters from calling objects is very useful and should remain. However, the definition of the default values and setup of the set of parameters on a class can be improved on, in particular as there is need to support multiple configurations, which may not have sensible corresponding default values, and the assignment of parameters for a given builder should be a fixed definition.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
BLUEPRINT uses a top level `Configuration` class, that contains all of the parameters available for a `Reactor`. From discussions with @je-cook, we would propose to introduce a set of `ParameterConfiguration` classes that are used to reflect the state of the parameterisation of a particular builder (or analysis). These give a more concrete definition of the parameterisation of a builder by acting as a schema. We should make it possible to look up the metadata for a given parameter from a set of central definitions, extend that allowed list of values, and validate that the parameters have been defined as expected. Parameters should be initialised with a None value by default to avoid unanticipated conflicts between different design studies.

title: Proposal: Add function to view geometry objects in 3-D
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When developing CAD design routines, it's really important to have rapid visual feedback to ensure that the functionality being developed is correct. The main way we do this at the moment in BLUEPRINT is to have some supporting functionality to view a BRep object(s) that is stored in memory (without having to save it to a CAD file and open it in a separate program). That might sound a bit "lazy" but I find it's a huge barrier to entry when developing and using the code. Especially if you're running in WSL.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would like there to be a simple function that can be called with a list of shapes, that shows those shapes in a 3-D window without leaving Python. Ideally, there would be a viewer where a whole bunch of different shapes can be viewed with context (name tags, colors, transparencies, etc.).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

The alternatives are:
* Do nothing. Continue saving files and viewing them in FreeCAD. I believe it will pose a barrier to entry, and I already see it as a considerable headache.
* Go back to pythonOCC...

**Additional context**

Perhaps the best thing about the previous pythonOCC approach used in BLUEPRINT was the rapid turnaround between writing a few lines of code and immediately viewing the result, without ever leaving the relative comfort of a Python terminal. Viewing an entire Reactor 3-D CAD with colors quasi-instantaneously is the highest value piece of PR we can aim for. If we can't do it with FreeCAD comfortably, I'd worry big time.

title: Winding pack design optimisations
body:
In GitLab by @CoronelBuendia on Jun 24, 2020, 15:51

CEA have a tool that does this, but it only supports their winding packs. It is a "proprietary" Excel spreadsheet... at least last time I saw it in action; it isn't automated, it needs to be used and frequently tweaked by an expert. All things considered it's fairly crude, if useful.

A group in SPC (specifically, Paul Scherrer Institut, Villigen) and another in ENEA have similar capabilities for their own winding pack designs. Although they don't call them tools as such, they have this "capability" which I imagine isn't entirely manual. The difficulty is, all of these are proprietary or "in-confidence" and the relevant knowledge doesn't really exist inside the organisation. These approaches also are specific to winding pack designs. Many of the conductors used in these designs have been tested in representative EM conditions, so there are quite a few experimental tweaking factors in these tools

The way winding packs are designed is to first have a guess on the size, sometimes using existing 1-D models (e.g. in PROCESS) or just saying current density = 12.5 MA/m^2, then have a stab in 2-D, and then check everything works in higher fidelity models (3-D FEA and other studies). We'd like to improve on the 2-D design step: replicating some existing capability in other labs, but improving and automating the process. We'd also like to prepare inputs for the higher fidelity models. It would need to run fairly fast (~seconds) and could potentially be used to make reduced-order models informing our simple guesstimates on things like "average winding pack current density" for a design.

* Inputs (from other parts of the BLUEPRINT code):
  * The geometrical cross-section of the winding pack, and the shape of the winding (circle for a PF coil, other shapes for a TF coil)
  * The currents required to be generated by the winding pack
  * The loads the winding pack is subject to
    * EM loadings
    * Magnetic fields across the winding pack (important for current density of the superconductor)
    * Neutronic heating deposited in the winding pack
    * Quench scenario
  * Winding pack parameters and design choices
    * Superconductor type (e.g. NbTi, Nb3Sn, etc.)
    * Winding type (pancake vs. layer)
    * Insulation thicknesses (inter-turn, inter-layer/inter-pancake, and ground)
    * Reference operation T (e.g. 4.2 K)
    * Coolant (e.g. He)
    * The desired T margin to quench (e.g. 1.5 K)
    * Maximum single conductor current rating (e.g. 100 kA)
    * Other thicknesses and values, etc.
  * Material properties
    * Superconducting properties and parameterisations
    * Steel properties
    * Coolant properties
* Tool activities:
  * Optimise the design of the winding pack for minimal size, so that it meets its current density requirement within the available space and withstands the applied loads
    * Determine the number of conductors in the winding and the layout of the conductors
    * Make the structures in the winding pack can withstand the stresses
    * Make the copper shunt fraction sufficient to withstand a quench
    * If the space available is too much / insufficient -> shrink / grow the WP geometry accordingly
  * Outputs for use in the BLUEPRINT code
    * Winding pack layout and 2-D geometry
    * Volumetric fractions of copper, superconductor, steel, insulation, ground insulation, etc.
    * Margin to the various constraints
  * Prepare inputs for higher-fidelity analyses
    * CAD models
    * Smeared material properties

title: equilibria optimisation speed gains
body:
In GitLab by @CoronelBuendia on Sep 7, 2020, 09:05

Major ideas to speed things up:

* optimise plasma profiles once (for the correct shape) and then save those parameters, converging with the frozen profiles
* carry opt position and current optimisations with fewer plasma shape constraints
  * Implement field direction constraints to stiffen up fits to plasma shapes (reduce size of constraint matrix)
* carry out position and current optimisations like nova used to do, which requires SOF and EOF "perfect" equilibria, which we could generate with 20 or so coils a la CREATE

all of the above would break API moderately, and so requires some thought... it would also require a fair amount of dev work, which I can't afford to do right now (if it ain't broke..).

The above could *significantly* accelerate the equilibria calculations (perhaps by a minute or two!)

title: Resisitive TF coils power loss
body:
In GitLab by @sebkahn on Sep 8, 2020, 17:40

## Description

Alongside superconducting magnets, resistive magnets are considered for STEP design. The PROCESS code already have this option inside to design it.

As the resistive power losses in the coil is invertly proportionnal to its cross-section, the inboard mid-plane section of the coil is thinner than the top one. This tapered geometry is considered and parametrized in PROCESS and would conflict with the TF coil ripple shaping and the future TF out of plane load optimisation in blueprint.

The resistive magnets cooling properties are also considered in PROCESS given as it sets the conductor temperature as a function of the coolant and conductor thermal properties the coolant velocity and the cooloing channel size and fraction.

Currently, all the PROCESS STEP designs are based on resistive magnet as @sebkahn did not managed yet to get a superconducting design working and fitting the available inboard mid-plane space.

## Proposal

Add the power required to cool and lost into the magnets in BLUEPRINT so it can take this into accout in the coil shaping for resistive magnets. For this, feel free to contact @sebkahn for any help.

The fact that the TF current carrying layer changes with the height is also an important bit to add. For no starting is available for now, sadly.

Ref : @CoronelBuendia 

Best regards    
S. Kahn

title: Heat flux onto the fw surfaces and fw shaping
body:
In GitLab by @DarioV86 on Nov 10, 2020 13:06

Steps to design the first wall profile according to the charged particle heat load:

## Approach A
- Inputs:
    - Equilibrium
    - SN or DN
    - First wall geometrical offset Delta_fw = 0.225m
    - Scrape-off layer power decay length lambda_q = 0.001m
    - Power crossing the SOL P_sol = 150 MW
    - Reactor major radius R_0 = 9m
    - Heat flux constraint q_fw_max = 1MW/m^2
    - Flux surface width in normalised flux delta_psi_norm = 0.01
- Outputs:
    - Optimised first wall shape
    - Heat fluxes on the first wall

1. Read an equilibrium file
    - Get the last closed flux surface
2. Make the preliminary first wall shape
    - Offset the LCFS by Delta_fw
    - Cut the FW below the X-point (if lower SN)
    - Cut the FW above the upper X-point (if upper SN or DN)
3. Analyse heat flux on first wall shape
    - Find all flux surfaces between the LCFS and the FW shape at the outboard mid-plane
    - Calculate the power carried by each flux surface at the outboard mid-plane q_0
    - Find all the intersections between each flux surface and the first wall shape
        - Find the first intersection starting from the OMP
        - Calculate the magnetic fields along each flux surface (all points)
        - Calculate the local parallel heat transport q_||
    - Calculate the angle between the first wall and the flux surface alpha_2d
    - Calculate the heat flux on the surface q_FW
4. Design the first wall shape
    - Find all segments of the FW where the heat flux is higher than q_fw_max
    - Move this segment away by translating it
    - Repeat all the steps with the modified first profile
 
Concern: The final shape could look weird and irregular with some segments that could make some "bumps" in the fw profile

## Approach B

- Inputs:
    - Equilibrium
    - SN or DN
    - First wall geometrical offset Delta_fw = 0.225m
    - Scrape-off layer power decay length lambda_q = 0.001m
    - Power crossing the SOL P_sol = 150 MW
    - Reactor major radius R_0 = 9m
    - Heat flux constraint q_fw_max = 1MW/m^2
    - Flux surface width in normalised flux delta_psi_norm = 0.01
- Outputs:
    - Optimised first wall shape
    - Heat fluxes on the first wall

1. Read an equilibrium file
    - Get the last closed flux surface
2. Get the starting point for the fw design
    - Point 0 at the OMP. 0.225m away from the lcfs. Picturing a polar system with origin in the current centroid, point 0 has theta=0 and ro=lcfs+0.225
    - Verify that q_|| is lower than material limit otherwise increase the distance from the lcfs
3. Design the wall point by point in order to have local heat flux within material limits
    - From the OMP decide to move either toward HFS or LFS.
    - e.g. toward the HFS.
    - Point 1 will be identified by theta=2° and ro=lcfs+0.225.
    - Calculate q_|| in that point. If it is lower than material limits, the segment 0-1 is the first segment of the fw, otherwise increase the distance from the lcfs

Concern: If I move point to point, I don't consider the shadowing effect. So I could find a point with an high heat flux and design the wall accordingly but that point could actually be shadowed

# Core plasma e.m. radiation heat on FW

## Description
Core γ radiation are bound to be a major source of heat in a tokamak first wall. Photons from the core arises from three mains phenomena:

1. Line radiation: Ions still carying electrons despite plasma temperature will emits photons when exited electrons get to lower energy orbits. This type of radiation mainly concerns high Z imprities and is documented in the following PROCESS and SYCOMORE papers [1-2]
2. Bremstrahlung: Rotating charged particles emits photons and must be integrated, becoming a important source of radiation [1-2]
3. Sycrotron: Additionnal radiation source I need to inderstand [3-4]
Radiation effect is planned to be dealt using Cherab [5] itself using RaySec [6] from a defined 2-3D source location.

## Plan

- [ ] Install Cherab
- [ ] Install RaySec (not mendatory be potentially usefull for future work)
- [ ] Parametrize a 2D source using the plasma magnetic closed surfaces
- [ ] Write a function calculating the heat flux generated by this source on the FW
- [ ] Work on a reduced model providing the radiation source term from plasma and impurity profiles (hard)

Best regards
Seb

Ref: @mkovari, @DanShort12, @CoronelBuendia, @DarioV86 and @byc-chan

[1] H. Lux, R. Kemp, D.J. Ward, M. Sertoli Fusion Engineering and Design 101 (2015) 42-51
[2] Johner Jean (2011), Fusion Science and Technology, 59:2, 308-349, DOI: 10.13182/FST11-A11650

title: Non convex hull regions for position optimisation of coils
body:
In GitLab by @je-cook on May 13, 2021, 14:58

The implemented position optimiser only works for Convex Hulls. To implement this for any polygon it is reasonably straight forward to normalise real space coordinates however converting to real space coordinates from normalised coordinates is not so straight forward.

To normalise and unnormalise the coordinates to avoid the limitation the only extra consideration is a plane that intersects your region boundaries more that twice. This currently raises an error within the code.

If that is true for normalising the coordinates you can effectively collapse the gaps in your region and normalise as if the region is a convex hull by subtracting the empty regions. 

- Possible downside optimisers may struggle with the non-linear relationship at region 'edges' 

Unnormalising coordinates is not so simple in 2D because you will have to iterate over an attempted unnormalisation checking at each point whether the current coordinate is within the region and subtracting the empty region, while expanding all other 'collapsed' sections of the region.

- The probable issue stems from whether you remove the x or z coordinate first because each change could lead to a different real position. If both are removed at the same time it could reduce the chance of this being an issue.

The current optimser limit included in the position optimiser already works for any polygon as implemented in `BLUEPRINT.geometry.inscribedrect`, although is not used at the moment (have a look at the convex flag). The only missing part is the position normalisation scheme.

This issue is just to store my current thoughts on the way forward if non convexhull regions are ever required. Feel free to comment and suggest improvements.

As mentioned in #420 a generic workflow for each external code should be a setup-run-teardown approach. This also is a collection of thoughts after a discussion with @DanShort12.

For complex systems that could depend on some external and some internal methods a [DAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph) could be set up that can be internal in bluemira and methods would be called based on what is defined for the run.

To achieve this we will need:

- A full list and dependency tree (essentially a DAG) of the current functions and methods with a minimal list that could be eg `make_equilibrium` etc similar to what is in `reactor.build` at the moment but flexibly defined.
- A generic in-run-out skeleton that will be inherited from for each new code adding for instance run and mock classes for process. Run then itself could be a complex set of nodes in the DAG.
   - in  would define any intrinsic things for input to codes
   - run would run a given instruction set eg create 'x' or run code 'y'
   - out would do some (probably extra) error checking on the output

All of this would facilite the use of bluemira for exploring a given parameter space.

title: Improve Green's Function Performance
body:
In GitLab by @NathanUKAEA on Jun 21, 2021, 13:29

In `greens_psi`, `greens_Bx` and `greens_Bz` the same factors, k, E(k) and K(k) are re-computed. I'd suggest placing this into one function that finds these once and uses them as required rather than re-calculating them multiple times for psi, Bx and Bz separately.

Also, the Scipy function uses interpolation for E and K, this may increase errors for values of k near 1, i.e. the field very close to the loop. Two methods to improve this may be to use the AGM calculation (Wikipedia has the simplest method and finds E and K simultaneously) and/or to use a different modulus, k_1 = (1-sqrt(1-k^2))/(1+sqrt(1-k^2)), this approaches 1 much slower for the same distance and so the AGM converges very quickly. Again Wikipedia has the general method for doing this. Maxwell himself seemed to have cracked this so there are plenty of other sources if required.

Lastly, the Green's functions are overloaded to deal with finite-sized wires using the d_xc and d_zc inputs, however, currently, they are only set to take into account the width only in z and not x. I'd suggest including both the d_xc and dz_c but for isolated coils, using Gaussian quadrature points and weights (evaluate at +/- 1/sqrt(3)*d_zc instead of +/- dz_c) so it requires the same 4 evaluations but gives 3rd order accuracy, rather than the trapezoid method which requires the same number of evaluations but gives 2nd order accuracy.

For fields far from the wire, the infinitely thin wire at the central point should be fine and the 3rd order corrections more than enough. However, for the meshed plasma loops, I would use the corner points (or other 'serendipity' nodes) instead of the Gaussian nodes as it will allow 2nd or higher quadrature with few extra function calculations but requires a slightly different method linking the plasma mesh to the green's function calculations instead of calculating them as separate loops i.e. cornerpoints will require 4*Nx*Nz but calculating them all together only requires slightly more than Nx*Nz.

More than happy to elaborate on this further if required.

title: Using Past Solutions in the Non-Linear Solver
body:
In GitLab by @NathanUKAEA on Jun 21, 2021, 14:19

In order to speed up parameter sweeps and optimisation, the non-linear solver should allow starting values of psi given from past solutions.

If only a small variation is applied, say for a parameter scan of the current from a single coil, this should allow the solver to start with a value that is pretty close to the solution and so require less Picard iterations to converge. A potential extension, if parameter sweeps are still being used and they're still taking a while, would be to use some extrapolation to speed this up further and attempt to predict a solution before it even begins.

An additional use is in the optimisation as Jacobian and Hessian matrices often require numerically calculated gradients which just move all parameters by a very small relative value. Making sure these are done with the previous result should require only a single iteration as the numerical differential assumes only a very small change to the system - if many iterations are required then the 'small relative value' probably needs to be reduced.

This isn't something I've looked at in the code and is just based on a conversation in the diverter design meeting. It could already be in there but just needs some setting up.

title: TF coil re-architecture
body:
In GitLab by @sebkahn on Jul 19, 2021, 16:36

## Description

It is geting more and more difficult to use the TF coil class in a user friendly way without bugs. Certain features are difficult to deal with, such as 
- The impossiblity to define a TF coil properly without any ripple optimization
- The code is really obscure and there, very few commenting and a lot of one letter variable name
- The way the 2D loops are made produce bad quality roundings making the CAD not fit for purpose (or the initial loops needs to be redone in the CAD maker ...). We may want to use CAD objects as well as loops there.
- We may want to expand the notion of segmented coil
- We may want to add the calculation of resisitivity and who knows, optimize on it with the ripple limit set as constraint.

## Proposal

The class has three main separate functionality
1. The class generation (`__init__`) that builds the geometry loops from params inputs and coil shape/WP/casing option selection. The parametrizaton can be done using dedicated class *a la* MIRA, as it seems to be the proper way and as conductor layout has common features for all coils. `__init__` calls `build_tf` that makes the geom loops
2. The optimization that call call the relevant optimizer object with all the needed setted up properly, runs the optimizer, run `build_tf` and `update_params` that update the value of all relevant params (for example these used in `__ini__`
3. The generation of a output param to be used to update the reactor system. The fonction must be returning a param object after calling `update_params` and a set of `@property` functions that calculate the relevant physical quantities such as stored energy, coil inductance, WP and case volumes, resistive heating (cost?). These function should be the same that are used by the optimizer.

Choosing what should be the inheritance based on is not that trivial as there quite a few combinatorics in the design options:
- Shape type 
- Conductor type/geometry
- Support structure geometry (case)
- Number of and type of joints, please note that having joints also allows to have different conductor types.

Conductor and support will be class in MIRA, so I suggest we go in that direction too, and the number of joints can be setup in a relatively generic manner. So I propose to base the inheritance on coil shape, this will also allow to break down the TF coil object better and avoid the sea of `if` statements.

Rem: The geometry loops should be both set in CAD and Loop objects, as loops seems to case **a lot** of troubles fairly easily.

This will be the right moment to **document** a bit better what is going on as well.

title: Improve robustness of make_mixed_wire / make_mixed_face
Ferromagnetic Modelling for In-Vessel Components
body:
In GitLab by @NathanUKAEA on Jul 26, 2021, 11:41

Some in-vessel components, such as the breeder blankets, may be made of magnetically permeable materials which could have a sizable effect on the plasma as they're in close proximity and similarly may effect the performance of nearby coils.

It's likely that the material will be magnetically saturated, so the magnitude of the magnetisation is set, but the direction of the magnetisation will be given by the sum-total of all fields present from the plasma and coils and its own field. This requires a self-consistent non-linear solver.

This is quite a development, and for the non-FEM demagnetisation tensor approach would require the following:
- Discretization of the material into elements of constant magnetisation (in a Cartesian sense, fixed radial magnetisation is still varying)
- Create demagnetisation tensor from analytic formula
- Calculate all fields inside material from external sources
- Non-linear solver to find self magnetisation
- Calculate stray field outside material from analytic formula to analyse effect

The stray field outside of a toroidally (near) continuous magnet is very small (micro-tesla) but, numerically speaking, this is a case of Catastrophic Cancellation, in that any one element actually creates a large field but the sum-total is near zero. This means that accuracy in the geometry may be vital - in the simulation, design and real-world construction. So a sensitivity analysis may be very useful.

title: Extract a separate Divertor class from the FirstWall class
body:
In GitLab by @DarioV86 on Sep 13, 2021, 16:59

Currently, the parent class `Firstwall` includes the child class `FirstWallSN` and the child class `FirstWallDN`. Both classes make a complete wall, comprehensive of divertor. However, whilst the first wall profile is optmised to reduce the heat flux, the divertor profile is merely "drawn", on the basis of simple geometrical inputs.

The idea is to isolate a class `Divertor` from the massive class `FirstWall`. In this way `FirstWall` would be semplified, and `Divertor` would be made in order to draw a flexible divertor, usable both for the SN and DN. For the DN, the upper divertor would be made by multiplying the z coordinates by -1.

In theory, the class `Divertor` should not need to be a child class. As to draw a divertor, only an equilibrium and some geometrical input are needed. The divertor doesn't need to know anything about the first wall.

The meeting point, on which the consistency between first wall and divertor needs to be held, is the divertor entrance. Divertor entrance that currently is led by the inputs `xpt_outer_gap` and `xpt_outer_gap`.

The main issue would be in deciding how the CAD should be handle. The first proposal (briefly discussed with Seb) would be to temporary leave the way how the cad is currently made. The CAD would be made after the class `Divertor` is invoked in the class `FirstWall`. As alternative, as FirstWall and Divertor would live separate, also the CADs could be made separately and only at the end merged. However, I believe @helen-brooks should have the last word about this key point.

P.S. I don't know how to add participants so I will tag them @sebkahn kahn @CoronelBuendia @je-cook

title: circuit_expander returning dictionary missing coils when coil.splittable == False in BLUEPRINT
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

`circuit_expander()` in the `CoilGroup` class entirely skips coils which have the `splittable` attribute set to `False`, which can lead to the coils dictionary output by `circuit_expander` to be empty or missing coils present in the `CoilGroup`.

This occurs because only the existence of the `splittable` attribute is tested for in the function, and not if it is set to `True` or `False`. The expected behaviour is seen if all the coils in the `CoilGroup` do not have the attribute `splittable`, or if all coils have the attribute `splittable` set to `True`.

## Proposed solution

Add a check to test if `coil.splittable` is set to `True` after testing for its existence, and if not, default to the behaviour used for coils that do not have the `splittable` attribute. 

## Additional context

This bug currently can lead to the output of `to_group_vecs()` being empty, which is used in when formatting the output of PF coil information for eqdsk files.

title: Patch to remove cad overlaps
body:
A patch to remove CAD overlaps. Point 2. is not regarded as a long term fix.

**1. Use 'miter' method in pyclipper offset in some places to avoid duplication of points in offset loops.**
Unrestricted mitering causes sharp spikes when applied to polygons with acute angles, and to avoid this pyclipper by default performs some squaring which creates an additional point, as explained in the documentation here: http://www.angusj.com/delphi/clipper/documentation/Docs/Units/ClipperLib/Classes/ClipperOffset/Properties/MiterLimit.htm
However, with a small tolerance on sufficiently smooth shapes, the squaring results in points that are essentially on top of each other. These duplicated point create numerical instability and tiny surfaces in the CAD that lack robustness. In this case it is perfectly reasonable to perform mitering without squaring, and avoids the creation of tiny surfaces.

**2. Avoid using make_mixed_face during CAD creation**
As noted in #219 (in comments) make_mixed_face seems to fail inconsistently. When make_mixed_face fails, the error is caught, and it falls back on make_face so that CAD is still generated, but a warning is printed. When it fails inconsistently between touching shapes, the resulting CAD contains overlaps (because different methods were used to generate the touching surfaces, even though they should be equivalent). Until make_mixed_face has been made more robust, it is proposed to reduce its usage. Even if this creates slightly less smooth CAD, (potentially  harder to mesh) it is at least self-consistent and thus more useful.

title: 2-D plotting of geometry objects
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

We must be able to plot one or multiple geometry objects on a plane, with associated colours.

Default colours should follow the existing colour palette (used previously in BLUEPRINT). The user should however be able to overwrite the colour palette, or specify a colour(s) for a geometry object(s) to be plotted.

Normally, we will need to plot on the x-z plane, but it should be made possible to plot on other planes.

The important thing is that the user is easily able to plot any `Component`, and that the way that this looks has an aesthetically pleasing default look.

## Proposed solution
As discussed last week, the proposed solution is to re-purpose the BLUEPRINT plotting functionality for the time being. Features of the MIRA plotting function (such as plotting on an arbitrary plane) should also be included.

* `Components` and other objects will have a `plot` method
* `Plotter` classes will be used to conceal the plotting logic, with the default plot options living on the `Plotter` class and not inside the `Component`
* The `Component.plot` method will expose the functionality to modify the plotting defaults to the user.

## Alternative solutions

We also discussed having a separate `plot_component` function in which all the plotting options are specified as inputs, or rather, overriding a set of defaults.

## Additional context

STEP users have been using the BLUEPRINT colour palette for several months, and it's pretty much the only thing they haven't raised an issue with :). Ideally, we should aim to preserve that "look", even if just initially.

title: Add a wide range of `GeometryParameterisation` implementations
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

In order to properly parameterise a reactor design, we need to support a wide range of different geometry parameterisations, that can be used to design and optimise different components.

In addition to the `PrincetonD` `GeometryParameterisation`, we should add:

* `PolySpline`
* `BackwardsPolySpline`
* `Johner`
* `Cunningham`
* `Manickam`
* `TripleArc`
* `PictureFrame`
* `TaperedPictureFrame`
* and other funky ST ones.

## Proposed solution

All of these parameterisations were implemented in BLUEPRINT using the now deprecated `Loop` functionality. These should be updated to follow the new `GeometryParameterisation` architecture and use the new way of making geometry using primitives.

## Alternative solutions

There are no viable alternatives; we need geometry paramterisations to be in primitive form.

title: Equilibria file saving according to COCOS-11 convention
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

Presently, when exporting equilibria to a file format (JSON or EQDSK), I'm not sure we actually follow the most common COCOS convention (https://crppwww.epfl.ch/~sauter/cocos/). 

We also treat loading of EQDSK files according to the header names, which for different codes (e.g. CREATE-*, EFIT++, etc.) are handled differently. It would be easiest to determine which COCOS convention such codes follow and use those to convert to our convention.

COCOS-11 is the most common standard it seems, so we should endeavour to implement that as the default setting. I believe it is what ITER uses.

## Proposed solution

Implement a strategy pattern for saving and loading EQDSKs, according to the COCOS conventions. I believe this can be done almost exclusively in the `file.py` of `equilibria`. There is one potential issue when treating combinations of negative/positive plasma current and negative/positive toroidal field. At the moment these are not actually treated in `bluemira`, but we will need to add this at some point.

## Alternative solutions

Figure out which COCOS convention we "follow" and claim that we export to a standard file format...

## Additional context

It is possible that COCOS-11 deviates from the standard global coordinate system which we use elsewhere in `bluemira`. We should only change how we treat equilibrium files, and not the general geometry coordinate convention.

title: CoilGroup methods failing with SymmetricCircuit members
body:
## Description

ForceField methods have also been broken by the changes to SymmetricCircuit, due to the assumption that the number of independently controlled coil currents (coilset._ccoils) is equal in size to the total number of coils (coilset.n_coils), which is not true when the coilset contains SymmetricCircuit members.

## Proposal

Rationalise how the number of "controlled"  coils and the real number of coils are treated in `CoilSet`.

`coilset.n_coils` should be the true number of physical coils in a `CoilSet`
`coilset.n_control_coils` should be the number of individually controlled current circuits in a `CoilSet`.

might be as simple as:

```python
@property    
def n_control_coils(self):
     return len(self._ccoils)
```

We need also to address how ForceField calculates force and field and jacobians in the case of symmetric circuits.

title: Agree, document, and enforce a `bluemira` unit convention
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

We are not fully consistent in units across `bluemira`. We've had some discussion regarding unit conventions, but we need to actually agree, document, and enforce a unit convention.

We've already resolved the topic of degrees vs radians: degrees as inputs and outputs to user-facing functionality

We also need to agree on units, e.g. SI or whatever, but sadly there are some pretty weird ones in the plasma physics and  neutronics worlds. So plasma densities in 10^19/m^2 or neutron fluxes in n/cm^2/s. I don't condone such units... but we do need to strike a balance between consistency and usability.

## Proposed solution

* Discuss and agree a unit convention.
* Document it and add it to the documentation somewhere
* Enforce it in the externally-facing functionality of the code

The latter will probably need to happen progressively...

## Alternative solutions

Live with unit quirks forever.

Proposed Unit Convention
=================

SI unit convention, (C or K), degrees not radians, no mega-milli-kilo-centi-pico stuff, except for kilogram..

* time: seconds [s]
* distance: metres [m]
* mass: kilograms [kg]
* current: Ampères [A]
* temperature: AHHH!
* amounts: moles [mol]
* angles: degrees [°]

We'll probably encounter some weird ones.

title: Primitive geometry offset feature
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

We need a way of offsetting *planar* geometry primitives at a constant thickness, preserving the type of geometry primitive of each of the boundary elements and propagating the label names.

Offsetting is non-trivial, and there are cases where the offset of a shape with `n` boundary wires may have fewer than `n` boundary wires.

For example, an equilateral triangle of edge length 1, with rounded corners at a radius of 0.1. In primitives this shape would be composed of 6 separates boundary elements: 3 straight lengths and 3 circle arcs. If one were to make an offset shape from this, with a thickness of -0.1, one would end up with an equilateral triangle of length 0.9, with only 3 boundary elements: 3 straight lengths. Such degeneracies should either be directly handled, or raise errors.

## Proposed solution

Develop a method to offset planar geometry primitives, which may or may not be composed of several boundary elements, in which the types of underlying boundary primitives and label names (if any) are propagated. 

Add an `offset` method to `BluemiraWire` (or a function in `geometry.tools.py`) that exposes the desired functionality

## Alternative solutions

We could continue to work with planar offsetting features available in BLUEPRINT, but they are relatively unstable, and would not lead to primitive geometry (unless one were to use the `MixedFaceMaker` to convert to primitives from a point cloud). This is not desirable.

## Additional context

3-D primitive offsetting is not immediately required, and I am assuming it adds appreciable complexity to developing this functionality. I suggest that we address it separately as and when we find we need it.

title: Replace first wall heat flux calculation with `bluemira` implementation
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

I'd like to replace @DarioV86 's heat flux calculation presently in `BLUEPRINT/systems/firstwall.py` with the `ChargedParticleSolver` in `bluemira/radiation_transport/advective_transport.py`.

## Proposed solution

The present API for the `ChargedParticleSolver` is as follows:

```python
solver = ChargedParticleSolver(equilibrium: Type[Equilibrium])
x_inter, z_inter, heat_flux = solver.analyse(first_wall_loop: Type[Loop])
```

The above would replace the calculation of the heat flux for a given equilibrium and geometry. However, I understand that some functions in the present implementation are also used to shape the first wall and divertor. These are exclusively related to extracting geometry information from equilibria, for which I am confident there are easy substituitions.

This transition offers two benefits:
* The concern of calculating the heat flux is separated from the concern of deciding what the geometry should look like. This should simplify the code in `firstwall.py`
* It used to run about 40 times faster (i.e. < 1 s) but since we've moved STEP over to the new `Loop` the gains are likely to not be as large. This should enable optimisations to be performed more readily.

I have already benchmarked the new solver with @DarioV86 and found identical results for the SN and DN test cases we ran.

## Alternative solutions

STEP continues to live with the present implementation.

## Additional context

The functionality in `firstwall.py` is presently being refactored. I will wait for this refactor to be merged before starting the transition.

title: 3D Display
body:
This PR introduces an implementation of a 3D displayer in the FreeCAD API, and then uses it to be able to display primitives, bluemira geometries, and components. As discussed, it uses something akin to dependency injection, but removes the decision on the type of display from the user by directly setting it in the constructor - only the options, which are common across all displayable objects, are passed into the constructor of the displayable object. Similarly, implements a mixin to handle making the object displayable and segregates off control of how the displaying is done to a separate `Displayer` class. There are certainly pros and cons to this approach, so will be useful to collect some feedback.

- Will the addition of new options when a new mixin is defined become too onerous or lead to mistakes in applying to child classes?
- I haven't extended the options to factory functions, opting instead for the user setting the options after creating the object - is that ok? Maybe we should just do the same for directly created objects rather than extending the constructor?
- The display essentially manipulates a coin3d `SoSeparator` to create the desired visual. In particular, when adding colour or transparency it needs to travers the `SoNode` tree to find any materials that need to be set. This can be slow already in 2D, so we'll need to see if it is prohibitive in 3D.

title: Geometry optimisation
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

We need a neat interface into geometry optimisation, using the already existing `GeometryParameterisation` and `OptVariables` infrastructure.

This interface should enable:
* Specification of a `GeometryParameterisation` with a set of `OptVariables`
* Normalised variable optimisation
* Constraints on combinations of variables, e.g. that x1 > x2, that can be used in gradient-based optimisers
* Additional user-specified miscellaneous constraints (e.g. TF ripple < max_ripple)
* Constraint(s) relative to other geometries, most probably via a single-valued signed distance function, or potentially a vector-valued signed distance function
* User-specified objective function

## Proposed solution

Create a `GeometryOptimiser` or `GeometryOptimisationProblem` class with methods for the specification of constraints and objectives. Add variable constraints on the `GeometryParameterisation`. Decide on an optimisation library, and set up an API that means easy interchange of algorithms and access to algorithm parameters.

Probably I will do a lot of this design first on MIRO, and then prototype, and then apply to a dummy problem. Taking the same approach that has been taken with the `_freecadapi` would probably be beneficial here, as it will allow the optimisation library to be replaced or interchanged if necessary.

## Alternative solutions
We could just try and port over the existing BLUEPRINT approach, but I am confident I can do better this time around, and address many of the weaknesses present in the existing approach. The fact that we now have primitive geometry could also help with the implementation of the geometry constraints in terms of signed distance functions etc.

## Additional context

There is probably a decision that needs to be made between NLOpt and scipy.optimize, too. I will try and stick to NLOpt, but some algorithms require that the Jacobians of the objective function and constraints be calculated, meaning that we have to write linear estimations of these when no analytical solutions are available. This is done under the hood in scipy, which is pretty much the only good thing about scipy.optimize.

title: Refactor `equilibria/coils.py`
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

Implement the general refactor of `coils.py` as discussed on MIRO:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/26097289/153381175-2443a98a-d3ba-4a13-bb53-eaf87b9e64d7.png)

The general ideas are as follows:
* `CoilGroup` shall be the new base class object, which `Coil`, `Circuit`, `SymmetricCircuit` and `CoilSet` inherit from
* A new mixin class shall be used to isolate all physical calculations associated with the existence of a `CoilGroup` (psi, Bx, Bz, etc.)
* `CoilGroup` shall remain ignorant of how they are being controlled or size-fixed
* `CoilSet` will be responsible for the control and size-fixing of coils, and have some utility methods for extracting useful subsets of coils inside the underlying `CoilGroup`


Now `SymmetricCircuit` inherits from `CoilGroup` objects, `CoilGroup` objects now may contain a mixture of `Coil` and `CoilGroup` objects within them, which each have their own (distinct) set of methods and attributes. This has introduced bugs such as #322 arising from calling methods and attributes existing in `Coil` objects that do not exist in `CoilGroup `objects. 

## Proposed solution

If `Coil` is made to inherit from `CoilGroup` as a special case (of size 1), then it can be assumed that all `CoilGroup` objects contain only `CoilGroup` objects of smaller size.

## Alternative solutions
`Coil` properties could be added separately to `SymmetricCircuit`, or all existing implementations updated to allow for either `Coil` or `CoilGroup` objects being present in `CoilGroup` objects. This would make the code more fragile when changes are made to how the coilset is handled.

title: Optimiser interface
body:
Introduces a thin wrapper layer around NLOpt, which is the selected optimisation library. An `Optimiser` class is introduced in the `utilities` module.

The API for the `Optimiser` is broadly speaking as follows:

```python
import numpy as np
from pprint import pprint

from bluemira.utilities.optimiser import Optimiser

def f_rosenbrock(x, grad):
    """
    The rosenbrock function has a single optimum at:
        f(a, a**2) = 0
    """
    a = 1
    b = 100
    value = (a - x[0]) ** 2 + b * (x[1] - x[0] ** 2) ** 2

    if grad.size > 0:
        # Here we can calculate the gradient of the objective function
        # NOTE: Gradients and constraints must be assigned in-place
        grad[0] = -2 * a + 4 * b * x[0] ** 3 - 4 * b * x[0] * x[1] + 2 * x[0]
        grad[1] = 2 * b * (x[1] - x[0] ** 2)

    return value

def f_constraint(constraint, x, grad):
    """
    Let's say that we only want to seach the space in which some combinations of
    variables are not allowed. We can implement this using just bounds, hence we need to
    add some constraints in.

    All we're effectively doing here is chopping the search space rectangle, and saying
    that:
        x1 + x2 < 3
        x2 - 2x1 > 1
    """
    constraint[0] = (x[0] + x[1]) - 3
    constraint[1] = (-2 * x[0] + x[1]) + 1

    if grad.size > 0:
        # Again, if we can easily calculate the gradients.. we should!
        grad[0, :] = np.array([1, 1])
        grad[1, :] = np.array([-2, 1])

    return constraint


results = {}
for algorithm in ["SLSQP", "COBYLA", "ISRES"]:
    optimiser = Optimiser(
        algorithm,
        2,
        opt_conditions={"ftol_rel": 1e-22, "ftol_abs": 1e-12, "max_eval": 1000},
    )
    optimiser.set_objective_function(f_rosenbrock)
    optimiser.set_lower_bounds([-2, -2])
    optimiser.set_upper_bounds([3, 3])
    optimiser.add_ineq_constraints(f_constraint, tolerance=1e-6 * np.ones(2))
    result = optimiser.optimise([0.5, -0.5])
    results[algorithm] = {
        "x": result,
        "f(x)": optimiser.optimum_value,
        "n_evals": optimiser.n_evals,
    }
```

closes #187 
closes #343

title: Divertor grazing angle inconsistency
body:
## Description of issue

For shallow divertor angles the separatrix curvature radius may generate some additionnal intersection before the expected impact point on the divertor tiles. This is problematic and it may be preferential to avoid it.

## Proposed solution

If the separatrix (or any other selected flux line) intersects the divertor plane before the parametrized target the following actions can be done
1. Increasing the poloidal plane tilt angle until having no intersection (little optimization)
2. Decrease the size of the divertor plate (straight line) until avoiding the unwanted intersection (little optimization)

Option 1 is probably the most robust, but ends up with an increased tilt angle while the second option preserve the tilt angle but may not always provided the expected result and probably leads to more complex divertor target shapes (non straight).

## Example 

Here, you can see that the divertor target angle is at 1 deg as expected, but that the separatrix curvature makes it cross before.


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/55831357/138290260-8b87b771-0bcf-488f-8293-543594be3292.png)
Figure 1: inboard divertor configuration. The expected target is defined by the intersection between the divertor wall shape (black line) and the divertor KoZ (green line). We can see the collision happends before the difertor target.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/55831357/138290147-56799601-6725-445a-b526-18a2df64325d.png)
Figure 2: inboard divertor configuration, zoom at the expected target location. The expected target is defined by the intersection between the divertor wall shape (black line) and the divertor KoZ (green line). We can observe the divertor target actually have the expected angle.

Best regards     
Seb

title: Initial Design/Builder implementation
body:
A very simple implementation of a builder and analysis. Certainly missing some functionality, but hopefully this can work as a basis to build out from.

Does the following:

- Adjusts parameters so that a template can be built in order to dynamically work out what parameters and needed for a builder and hence analysis.
- Implements a very simplistic component manager to handle adding and accessing components.
- Implements a `Builder` abstract base class that makes components for a given target path (corresponding to the path in the component manager).
- Implements a `MakeParameterisedShape` builder, just to have something to play around with - allows `GeometryParameterisation`s to be parameterised and then build as-is.
- Implements a simple analysis that can determine a set of builders to run from a provided configuration.
- A few tests to demonstrate the above.

Does not do the following:

- Implement an analysis chain that also allows subsequent builders to pull in components. In particular, does not optimisation to the shapes that are passed in - likely would need a new builder class that updates the parameterisation corresponding to the optimisation performed.
- Implement an analysis stage (runner?) to run systems codes or equilibria (even our internal one) and store the output in either parameters or generic attributes (maybe dynamically created on the analysis class?) - could use a 'source' / 'sink' structure to then allow dynamic attributes to be accessed in subsequent steps.

## Description
In STEP reactor the divertor loop section of the first wall contains points which are very close together - with a resolution of ~ 10^-5 (see screenshots below). Later, when the imprint and merge operation is performed upon the CAD ( which happens typically with a tolerance higher than this ~10^~4 ) an error is raised because

title: Update Heat Flux Model to handle upper single null and not ideal double null
body:
Currently the heat flux calculaltion model handles lower single null divertor configurations and "ideal" double null divertor configurations. "Ideal", meaning primary and secondary separatrix perfectly overlapped.

The first part of the update would be addressed to upper single null divertor configurations. 
Referring to **_[T. Takizuka et al 2009 Nucl. Fusion 49 075038]_** , for the upper null, the stagnation point (V parallel equal to 0) can be assumed to be located symmetrically at the bottom. Unlikely the lower null, where (as described in our model) the stagnation point is assumed to be at the mid-plane.

The second and major update would be addressed to double null divertor configurations, with primary and secondary separatrices not overlapping.
Referring to **_[D. Brunner et al 2018 Nucl. Fusion 58 076010]_** , in double null divertor configurartions, most likely primary and secondary separatrix do not overlap. The distance between the two separatrices is used to quantify the degree of double-nullness.

When the distance between primary and secondary separatrix is not equal to zero, the double null configuration can be seen as a combination of a lower and upper single null divertor configuration (here the necessity of implementing upper single null divertor configuration).
The not ideal double null configuration  affects the power sharing between upper and lower divertor, and inner and outer divertor legs.

Being the primary divertor the one that is directly connected to the LCFS, the power crossing **ONLY** the primary separatrix **ONLY** goes to primary divertor targets. 
From the primary scrape-off layer, the power crossing the secondary separatrix is split, and goes towards upper and lower divertor.

The current model splits 50%-50% between upper and lower divertors, and 90%-10% between inner and outer divertor legs. Such power sharing is in agreement with Brunner's conclusions at double-null (He refers as double-null what we call ideal double-null).
Moreover, to address the 10% of power to the inner legs, our model foresees a secondary particle source at the Inboard Mid-Plane (IMP). This assumption is not made in Brunner's model, but it serves the cause.

My suggestion is to implement the Brunner's model for double null divertor configurations.
However, based on the question "how far could we be from a ideal double null divertor configuration?", that in turn gives "Is it worth updating the current model?", I would interrogate experts such as Stuart Henderson, Ryoko Osawa and Michael Kovari.

My apologies if @alexanderianblair knows the subject and I didn't include him in the "experts". I am just not sure about that.
@sebkahn 
@alexanderianblair 
@je-cook 

[https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0029-5515/49/7/075038/meta?casa_token=J_huJiXddv4AAAAA:BeCddVX5-2szua17E3RTD-mTiMeObZST2B9zB3pwAdSP6gYaJJRRfjiuzca7Y28QMfwoiapa4XU](url)

title: Remove copy() aliases for deepcopy()
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

In many modules, many classes (such as `Coil,` `CoilGroup,` `MagneticConstraintSet,` `Equilibrium,` `FluxSurface` among others) have a custom `copy()` method that is an alias for `copy.deepcopy()`. This is undesirable, as this confuses the python shallow and deep copy methods, and makes it more difficult to track when new copies of objects are being created. 

In the worst case, this confusion could lead to unexpected behaviour, where pointers may be pointing to different objects due to a `deepcopy` being performed when a shallow `copy` was expected.

## Proposed solution

Remove these methods, and just use `copy` and `deepcopy` from the `copy` module directly.

title: Add an EquilibriumAnalyser class to group Equilibrium analysis methods
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

Methods to extract useful properties of `Equilibrium` objects (requiring analysis of the stored `Equilibrium` data) are currently scattered in different modules, making them hard to locate, and leading to similar methods being used in multiple places.

For example - `get_separatrix` is called from `Equilibrium`, methods to extract the locations of the inboard and outboard midplane are used in larger methods at various places within `firstwall.py`, and identification of primary O and X points is repeated in several modules. Large parts of the new `ChargedParticleSolver` (#413) also perform such processing of `Equilibrium` objects, which should be centralised. 

## Proposed solution

Provide a new `EquilibriumAnalyser` class that provides methods to extract useful parameters from `Equilibrium` and associated `FluxSurface`s. Any use of these properties - such as in `firstwall.py`, `optimiser.py`, or elsewhere in `equilibrium.py`, should then call the `EquilibriumAnalyser` and not attempt to extract information from `Equilibrium` directly. New analysis tools and methods to extract `Equilibrium` properties can then be more easily provided via extensions to `EquilibriumAnalyser`.

`EquilibriumAnalyser` should be strictly read-only, and should not modify the `Equilibrium` it acts upon or change its behaviour. 

## Alternative solutions

Extend `FluxSurface` directly with methods that extract these properties, and use these `FluxSurface` methods instead anywhere where `Equilibrium` properties are needed. I'm less keen on this idea, as `FluxSurface` can otherwise be an encapsulated object that should kept separate from these extra responsibilities.

## Additional context

This will also be convenient for future FBE figures of merit that rely on the current `Equilibrium` state, as there will be less reproduction of effort if the existing approaches in `firstwall.py` can be used.

title: `make_divertor_target` SOL and PFR swaping
body:
## Describe the bug

The SOL and PFR divertor targets length parametrization are often swaped. 

## Steps to reproduce

Run SPR-017 (or probably any STEP designs).

## Expected behaviour

We expect the PFF length to size the PFR and the SOL to size the SOL.

## Background

The tangeant to the separatrix loop is determined in the `get_tangent_vector` function, using loop point indexes. This makes the process dependent on the way the loop indexes are setup. As I understand (plz check and correct me if I am wrong @DarioV86) the tangeant is defined using the separatix point and the  closest n-1 point. In case of different order the notion of PFR and SOL as well as the angle are swapped.

This issues is partly soleved by changing the angle of the rotation and swapping the SOL and PFR point *a posteriori*. This is all good but the length needs swapping too there, hence the bug as it is not done with the current logic.

## Proposed solution

Swap the points **before** the target length are set. In addition the swapping can be performed with a rotation of 180 deg using the strike point as centre for the rotation.

Hope this solves the observed issues !

Best regards      
Seb

title: Standardise the shape of point arrays
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

In several places in geometry, and elsewhere in some solvers, we are working with numpy `ndarray`s representing clouds of sequentially connected points.

At present, there is an unfortunate mixture of `xyz.shape = (3, N)` and `xyz.shape = (N, 3)`. Accessing a point or a coordinate vector is therefore different depending on how the array was made and is problematic in use and development. 

The fact that these sequentially connected points do not have a clockwise or counter-clockwise convention also causes issues in some places.

```python
  separatrix = JohnerLCFS(
      {
          "r_0": {"value": 9},
          "z_0": {"value": 0},
          "a": {"value": 9 / 3.1},
          "kappa_u": {"value": 1.65},
          "kappa_l": {"value": 1.8},
      }
  )

print(separatrix.create_array().shape)               # --> (3, 203)
print(separatrix.create_shape().discretize().shape)  # --> (100, 3)
```

## Proposed solution

At the very least, we need to standardise the shape of the coordinate arrays across the code-base. I personally prefer (3, N), as it unpacks with `x, y, z = *xyz` enables functions to be called with (*xyz).

Making a polygon and other primitives should also be standardised, so we'd have to choose between:

```python
make_polygon(points=[[0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [2, 0, 0]])
```
and 
```python
make_polygon(x=[0, 1, 2], y=[0, 0, 0], z=[0, 0, 0])
```

## Alternative solutions

This isn't going to be popular, but the `Loop` class in BLUEPRINT was originally made to address these issues, and provide easy access to point and coordinate vectors by indexes and `.x`, `.y`, `.z`, `.xyz` attributes. I'm not saying that we use the `_deprecated_loop.Loop` class, but this is a very real problem, and there is already a solution in the code-base. We could have a very reduced subset of `Loop` functionality for coordinate arrays that treats dimensioning and orientation self-consistenly. Of course, many of the other features of `Loop` are now superseded by other functionality, so we wouldn't need much. For me, and this might sound tragic, but there is also a "readability" gain from `xyz_array[:, 1]` to `points.y` and `xyz_array[0, :]` to `points[0]`

title: Add inequality constraints to `GeometryParameterisation`
body:
This is something I've been wanting to do for a while, and I'm hoping it will pave the way for broader bounds on the `OptVariables`.

Basically, we sometimes need constraints on relations between variables, which may or may not be bounded.

Easiest concept: for the PrincetonD, we have x1 and x2, where we really want x1 < x2. If we don't set our bounds cleverly, say:

```python
x1 = BoundedVariable(value=3, lower_bound=2, upper_bound=10)
x2 = BoundedVariable(value=5, lower_bound=4, upper_bound=20)
```
The optimiser could easily try and set x1=10 and x2=4, which would raise an error.

I've implemented these for the PrincetonD and the TripleArc (which, because this didn't exist previously, was immensely fragile to optimisation).

I didn't want to do all the `GeometryParameterisations` in one go, because I wanted to trial this concept. I'm not 100% happy with it, because it feels borderline spaghetti-like.

I'm also not sure if it is a good idea to enforce shape constraints (if they are present) in a `GeometryOptimisationProblem`. I kind of feel they should be intrinsic to the `GeometryParameterisation`, which should work "out of the box", but in many cases you can protect against these constraints by clever use of bounds. Like above in the PrincetonD, you could just set the bounds and not worry about using these inequality constraints. It'd be fine if there wasn't a hit on performance, but for non-gradient based optimisers in particular there are clearly more constraints that need to be evaluated (without analytical gradients) and performance deteriorates.

Keen for suggestions and opinions on this one.

body:
The initial implementation of the PROCESS interface used a Reactor object to pass information around. This doesn't make for good encapsulation and also ties the functionality into legacy BLUEPRINT objects.

title: Add coupling to PLASMOD and fixed boundary equilibrium
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

At present, our free boundary equilibrium are solved with input custom profiles, or profiles constrained for `I_p`, `beta_p` and `l_i`.

There is no information relating to actual plasma profiles: the flux functions `p'` and `FF'` are used as mathematical tools, but do not harbor any relation to plasma transport.

We need a way to pass from the PLASMOD 1.5-D transport and fixed boundary equilibrium solver to a asymmetric 2-D fixed boundary equilibrium, using the `p'` and `FF'` from PLASMOD, which treats these more thoroughly (i.e. with a physics basis).

## Proposed solution
Add a 2-D finite element fixed boundary equilibrium solver.
Add coupling to PLASMOD with an asymmetric separatrix, constraining `kappa_95`, `delta_95`, `R_0`, `A`, such that we can reach an asymmetric fixed boundary equilibrium with PLASMOD profiles, which can later be used in free boundary equilibrium calculations.

Iterations between PLASMOD and the 2-D fixed boundary equilibrium will be required.

## Alternative solutions

Continue to use custom profiles, or constraining profiles with plasma integrals. The proposed approach will be superior from a consistency perspective.

title: WIP: Add a TF coil builder
Wire discretisation is sometimes CW, sometimes CCW
body:
## Description of issue / requirement to address

When we discretise wires to numpy arrays, we do not do any treatment on those wires. Apparently, discretisation does not result in consistent orientations, which unfortunately leads to some really difficult to diagnose problems.

For example:

```python
from copy import deepcopy
from bluemira.geometry.parameterisations import PrincetonD
from bluemira.geometry.tools import offset_wire
from bluemira.geometry._deprecated_tools import check_ccw

x_tf_wp_center = 3.2
parameterisation = PrincetonD(
    {
        "x1": {"value": x_tf_wp_center, "fixed": True},
        "x2": {"lower_bound": 10, "value": 14, "upper_bound": 18},
        "dz": {"lower_bound": -0.5, "value": 0, "upper_bound": 0.5, "fixed": True},
    }
)

wire = parameterisation.create_shape()
array = wire.discretize(byedges=True)

print(check_ccw(array[:, 0], array[:, 2]))  # True

dx_values = [-0.25, 0, 0.25]
dy_values = [-0.4, 0, 0.4]

new_wires = []

for dx in dx_values:
    new_wire = offset_wire(wire, dx)

    for dy in dy_values:
        temp = deepcopy(new_wire)
        temp.translate((0, dy, 0))
        new_wires.append(temp)

for w in new_wires:
    array = w.discretize(byedges=True)
    print(w._orientation)  # They're all _Orientation.FORWARD
    print(check_ccw(array[:, 0], array[:, 2]))  # First 6 True, last 3 False
```
The last three are in the positive quadrant, and somehow go clock-wise, which could either be a result of the offsetting or a result of the translation, or both, don't know.

If you put those arrays into e.g. a Biot-Savart solver, which for better or for worse assumes there is some consistency in terms of CW/CCW, then you get no errors (atm) but you certainly do get weird results. The direction of the sets of the coordinates feeds into the direction of the currents.

## Proposed solution

At the very, very least, we need to have some consistency (even choice) in terms of the CCW-nature of numpy arrays that describe ordered sets of coordinates. 

## Alternative solutions
In my mind, we need a class that behaves a hella lot like a numpy array, but specifically for 3-D sets of coordinates, in which you can choose the CW/CCW orientation of the points, and access them easily via `.x, .y, .z, .xyz`, etc.

This is issue is just another reason to consider this, along with #438
